findings.existing_test_gap: The selftest fixtures (from line 117) build cards via _card(senses, ...) with non-empty sense lists; no fixture covers records with an empty senses list or source_senses <= 1.
findings.fix_boundary: Add an unconditional `osc == 0` HARD issue and treat `want == []` as coverage None/0 rather than 1, then re-assert JS/Python agreement on the new fixtures.

corrections: The invariant statement is fine, but the reachability claim is wrong. Correct form: "coverage is reported as 1.0 and osc==0 is unguarded when skeleton_tokens is empty — unreachable on real PWG data (0/123,366 records mask to zero placeholders; the only zero-token lane is the synthetic non-promotable dq_canary_puregloss fixture, which has source_senses=3 and is caught by the shortfall gate). Hardening-only, not a live A/B gate hole."

findings.title: safe_id() collapses two distinct key1 values onto one xml:id / RDF subject — exactly one live collision pair (`U` vs `U~`), and it is NOT the cause of the 12,374 duplicates in the shipped artifact
findings.invariant: One exported entry = one source headword. Two distinct key1 values must never share an xml:id (XML ID uniqueness) or an IRI (RDF subject identity), or the graph silently merges two lexemes.
findings.failure_scenario: key1 `U` and key1 `U~` both go through `re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z0-9_]+','_', ...)` → segment `U`. The disambiguating counter is `idn[key1] += 1` — keyed on the RAW key1, not on the emitted slug — so both are the first occurrence of their own key1 and both emit the suffix-free form. In the shipped release/ontolex.ttl this produces TWO `pwg:U a ontolex:LexicalEntry` blocks (lines 74402 and 74419) whose `ontolex:canonicalForm` writtenReps are `"U"@sa-Latn` and `"U~"@sa-Latn`; after RDF parsing they are ONE entry with two canonical forms and the union of both sense lists, and `pwg:U_sense_1` receives triples from whichever headword emitted it. In release/tei_lex0.xml the same two headwords both carry `xml:id="pwg-U"` (line 40716 has `<orth>U~</orth>`). A consumer resolving pwg:U cannot tell the two lexemes apart; a consumer keyed on xml:id silently drops one.
findings.evidence: export_interop.py:36-37 `def safe_id(s): return re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z0-9_]+', '_', str(s or 'x')).strip('_') or 'x'`. export_interop.py:134-135 `idn[key1] += 1  # unique xml:id across same-key1 homograph entries` / `cid = 'pwg-%s' % safe_id(key1) + ('' if idn[key1] == 1 else '-%d' % idn[key1])` — the counter is indexed by key1 while the collision happens after safe_id. Same shape at export_interop.py:158-159. The defect is already named in the sibling emitter: export_lod.py:89-92 `"""Injective segment encoder … Reversible enough that two distinct keys never collapse to the same IRI segment (the old ``safe_id`` merged them)."""` — but make_edition_cut.py:23 `INTEROP = ('tei_lex0.xml','ontolex.ttl','reverse_index.jsonl')` still ships export_interop's output, not export_lod's.
findings.existing_test_gap: No test asserts injectivity of safe_id or uniqueness of emitted xml:id/IRI. tests/ has no export_interop test at all; ci.yml:399 exports a single-card fixture, where a two-key collision cannot occur. The fix already exists in export_lod.iri_local but was never back-ported and no test forbids the regression.
findings.fix_boundary: export_interop.py: key `idn` on the emitted slug (`safe_id(key1)`), or replace safe_id with export_lod.iri_local. Regenerating release/tei_lex0.xml + release/ontolex.ttl afterwards is required — the collision is baked into the committed bytes.

corrections: Three corrections, all narrowing the finding rather than negating it. (1) The evidence conflates two independent defects. The shipped release/tei_lex0.xml has 14,091 duplicate xml:ids, but only ONE (pwg-U) comes from safe_id non-injectivity; the other 14,090 are same-key1 homographs that the idn counter would have suffixed. Zero suffixed ids exist anywhere in either shipped artifact, proving they were generated by a pre-counter build and committed stale in the very commit (5869f25ee) that added the counter. So fix_boundary's "regenerating is required" is right, but regeneration alone fixes 14,090 duplicates from a different cause and only 1 from this one — and conversely, fixing safe_id without regenerating fixes nothing shipped. (2) Blast radius is one pair, not a general merge hazard: key1 is SLP1, only 11 of 106,082 distinct keys contain a rewritable char, the only such chars are '|' and '~', and only U~ collides — via .strip('_') folding a trailing '~' away onto plain 'U'. The failure_scenario's "a consumer resolving pwg:U cannot tell the two lexemes apart" is literally true but is the entire extent of the damage, not an instance of a pattern. (3) The merged entry U~ emits no glosses, so the RDF consequence is a spurious second canonicalForm plus an empty sense_0 on pwg:U — not a union of two populated sense lists, and no translated content is lost. Severity P1 -> P2 accordingly.

Two refinements to the finding's prose, neither of which weakens it. (1) Blast radius in the current corpus is exactly ONE collision pair — `U` vs `U~` — out of 106,082 distinct key1; I measured every row, so the defect is real but narrow in count. Its severity comes from the consequence, not the count: a single duplicate xml:id makes the whole 22.9 MB `release/tei_lex0.xml` unparseable by any xml:id-enforcing parser (lxml refuses outright), and in RDF it merges two lexemes into one subject. (2) The finding implicitly attributes the shipped file's damage to safe_id. In fact `release/tei_lex0.xml` contains 12,374 duplicate xml:id values (14,091 entries lost to collision), and the file contains ZERO `-N`-suffixed ids — i.e. the committed artifact was generated BEFORE the homograph counter at :134-135 existed. Only 1 of those 12,374 (pwg-U) survives the current code; the other 12,373 are a separate, larger staleness defect in the committed release bytes. The fix_boundary's "regenerating release/tei_lex0.xml + release/ontolex.ttl is required" is therefore even more necessary than stated, but for two independent reasons. Also worth adding to the fix boundary: `validate_interop.py:21-30` is the natural place to add the uniqueness assertion — it currently passes colliding output because ElementTree ignores xml:id uniqueness.

findings.lead_adjudication: CONFIRMED by both lenses but materially narrowed, and the narrowing matters because the original finding conflated two independent defects. Measured, by me and by both verifiers: of the 12,374 duplicated xml:id values in the shipped release/tei_lex0.xml, 12,373 have IDENTICAL <orth> — the same key1 emitted repeatedly, which is the STALE-ARTIFACT defect (L-9) — and exactly ONE, pwg-U for orth 'U' and 'U~', is a genuine safe_id collapse. So safe_id explains 1 of 12,374, not the bulk, and the finding's claim that 'the homograph counter never disambiguates them' is false of the current code: export_interop.py:134-135 does uniquify same-key1 entries, as an executed run over the full 120,172-card set confirms (1 collision, not 12,374). What survives at P2 is the real safe_id defect: `idn` is counted on the RAW key1 while the id is built from safe_id(key1), so two distinct keys that collapse under the regex get independent counters and therefore the same id, with no error. One pair today, and nothing prevents the next.

findings.title: export_ontolex tags every exported sense @ru regardless of its actual language — German, English and Sanskrit strings ship as Russian-language literals
findings.invariant: An RDF language tag is a factual claim about the literal it decorates. A multi-source card whose senses come from German dictionary glosses, Russian translations and Sanskrit corpus lemmas cannot carry one language tag for all of them.
findings.failure_scenario: card_glosses returns four heterogeneous row kinds — `attested_senses.dict` glosses (line 92-94, source dictionaries incl. `fri`, whose text is Latin/English), `kow_reference` (line 95-96), `corpus_lexicon.strata[].renderings[].lemma`, i.e. bare Sanskrit/Russian lemma forms (line 97-100), and the RU store translations (line 110-114) — and export_ontolex writes all of them through the single line `ontolex:usage "%s"@ru`. The shipped release/ontolex.ttl:22 has `ontolex:usage "I a- pron., cf. a-tas, a-tra &c.;"@ru` (sourceRef "fri") and :25 `"II a- augment;"@ru`. Any SPARQL filter of the shape `FILTER(lang(?u)='ru')` — the obvious way to extract the Russian layer from this graph — returns the German/English/Sanskrit material too. The TEI sibling loses the information the other way: export_tei:140-141 emits `<sense source="..." n="..."><def>...</def></sense>` with no xml:lang at all, so the language is simply absent.
findings.evidence: export_interop.py:170 `f.write('  ontolex:usage "%s"@ru .\n' % ttl(text))` — unconditional, inside `for i, (source, ref, text) in enumerate(senses, 1)`. export_interop.py:90-100 shows `source` already distinguishes 'dict' / 'kow' / 'corpus_lexicon' from the translation rows at :112-114, so the language is knowable at the point of emission and is discarded.
findings.existing_test_gap: No test parses the emitted Turtle or asserts anything about language tags; validate_ontolex (validate_interop.py:33-42) only counts a substring, so a graph in which every literal is mislabelled validates. ci.yml:399-400 runs both over a one-card fixture whose only dict gloss happens to be Russian, so the fixture cannot surface the mismatch.
findings.fix_boundary: export_interop.py export_ontolex: map the `source` value already carried by card_glosses to a language tag (approved_translation/kow → ru, dict → per-source language from corpus_gate, corpus_lexicon lemma → sa-Latn) and emit that; add xml:lang on the TEI <def>.

corrections: Title and failure scenario must be narrowed. (1) No German material is in this graph — the German lexicon ships via a different exporter (release/pwg_de_lexicon_h1350_demo.ttl), not export_ontolex. (2) `kow_reference` and `corpus_lexicon.strata` rows are dead code paths for the real store: 0 occurrences in 120,172 assembled cards, and 0 non-"dict" termElement values in the shipped 37,409-literal ontolex.ttl. Those branches are correctness-unverified but not currently reachable with data. (3) `fri` is a Russian-language source, not "Latin/English": 6,549 of its 6,771 literals contain Cyrillic. (4) The true defect is exactly 227 literals (0.61%) that are Latin-script cross-reference stubs mislabelled `@ru`; the SPARQL over-return is 0.6% noise, not a mixed-language layer. The valid, unconditional part of the finding is the missing source→language mapping at export_interop.py:170 and the missing xml:lang at export_tei:140-141, plus the real test gap that validate_ontolex never parses tags — but that is a latent-hardening item, not a shipped multi-language corruption.

findings.title: The citable TEI/OntoLex export ignores the per-sense `publishable` rights flag it is handed, so a rights-unconfirmed source would ship into the release
findings.invariant: A sense the rights model marks non-publishable must not appear in a citable release artifact; that is the only reason the flag is carried on the card at all.
findings.failure_scenario: card_glosses iterates `card['attested_senses']['dict']` and emits every entry whose `gloss` is truthy, never reading `d['publishable']` — the field assemble.py:174 writes onto each dict sense precisely so the export can honour it (`'publishable': g.get('publishable', False)`). corpus_gate.py:84-85 marks `grin12` and `grin3` as `{'publishable': False, 'status': 'rights-unconfirmed', 'basis': 'evidence-only pending rights check'}`, and corpus_gate.lookup_specialist:190-191 attaches those glosses with the flag set. The moment a specialist-glossary sense reaches a card — the code path exists and is wired — its text is written into release/tei_lex0.xml and release/ontolex.ttl and then copied by make_edition_cut into the sha256-pinned citable edition, with no filter, no warning and no count. Today's release happens to contain only the four publishable codes (koch/fri/kna/smirnov), so the leak is latent, not fired; the guard, however, does not exist anywhere in the export path. The counterpart export in the same repo does this correctly by construction (export_de_edition quarantines and reports counts in its manifest, lines 657-704), which is the shape this one lacks.
findings.evidence: export_interop.py:92-94 `for d in card.get('attested_senses', {}).get('dict') or []:` / `    if d.get('gloss'):` / `        rows.append(('dict', d.get('code') or d.get('source') or 'dict', d.get('gloss')))` — `publishable` is never referenced in the file (no occurrence of the string). Producer side: assemble.py:174 `'publishable': g.get('publishable', False)`; corpus_gate.py:84-85 and :89-90 `def publishable(code): return RIGHTS.get(code, {}).get('publishable', False)`.
findings.existing_test_gap: No test asserts that a non-publishable dict sense is excluded from the interop export. src/fixtures/assembled_card.fixture.jsonl — the only input CI feeds the exporter (ci.yml:399) — contains exactly one dict sense with `"publishable":true`, so the false branch is never taken in any test or CI run.
findings.fix_boundary: export_interop.py card_glosses: skip dict rows where `d.get('publishable')` is falsy unless an explicit --include-restricted preview flag is set, and return/print the skipped count so the drop is never silent (mirroring export_de_edition's `quarantined_rows` manifest field).

corrections: The finding's mechanism claim is wrong: specialist (grin12/grin3) glosses are NOT wired into `attested_senses['dict']`. `lookup_specialist` feeds only `corpus_gate.build_card()['specialist_glosses']` (corpus_gate.py:533), a card shape with no `attested_senses` at all and which no exporter consumes. The only producer of `attested_senses['dict']` is assemble.py:172-174, fed exclusively by `cg.lookup()` over INDEP = koch/kna/fri/smirnov, all of which are `publishable: True`. The scenario therefore needs a source-code change, not data, and is not "latent but wired". The accurate residual defect is much narrower and P3: `publishable()` returns False for any code absent from RIGHTS, so if someone later adds a code to INDEP without a RIGHTS row, the export would silently ship it — an argument for a cheap assertion, not a rights-leak finding. The same missing filter also exists at export_lod.py:272, which the finding does not mention.

findings.title: changelog-lint gate only inspects the ROOT changelog; RussianTranslation/CHANGELOG.md is unguarded and already carries the exact defect
findings.invariant: The duplicate-entry gate must cover every changelog the repo maintains — a gate that passes while the defect it names is live in a tracked changelog is a false green.
findings.failure_scenario: `main()` resolves `repo = dirname(dirname(__file__))` (the repo root) and picks the first of ('CHANGELOG.md','CHANGELOG.md','Changelog.md') that exists there; it never walks subdirectories. This repo has four tracked changelogs (`git ls-files | grep -i changelog`), of which the root `CHANGELOG.md` is checked and `RussianTranslation/CHANGELOG.md` — the one `review_changelog_guard.py:12` makes mandatory to touch — is not. Running find_duplicates on it right now returns 3 duplicated entries / 6 copies: the whole `### H429 — PWG page/column co-location index` block is present twice inside the same `## [1.9.9] - 2026-07-14` section (lines 3751-3764 and 3795-3808). That is precisely the Systema-Sanscriticum#684 fan-out class the module docstring (lines 1-15) exists to catch, live, while `changelog-lint.yml:31` reports green.
findings.evidence: scripts/changelog_duplicate_bullets.py:169-174 `repo = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))` / `path = next((os.path.join(repo, n) for n in CHANGELOG_NAMES if os.path.isfile(...)), None)`. Measured: `find_duplicates(open('RussianTranslation/CHANGELOG.md').read())` -> dupe_entries=3, copies=6, hits at lines [3752,3796], [3761,3805], [3764,3808]; `awk` confirms both copies sit under the same `## [1.9.9] - 2026-07-14` heading (line 3254). `python scripts/changelog_duplicate_bullets.py` exits 0.
findings.existing_test_gap: The script has no selftest and no test file; `.github/workflows/changelog-lint.yml:31` runs it bare, so the only assertion is its exit code — which is 0 because it was pointed at a file that happens to be clean. Nothing asserts that the set of files checked equals the set of tracked changelogs.
findings.fix_boundary: scripts/changelog_duplicate_bullets.py main() — enumerate `git ls-files` matches for CHANGELOG_NAMES at any depth instead of the root only, and fail on the union. No change needed in the workflow.

corrections: Two corrections, neither fatal. (a) Severity is somewhat inflated: P2 overstates it. The blast radius is a false-green CI badge plus one duplicated documentation block — no data, runtime, or user-facing effect, and the duplicate is inert prose in an archived 1.9.9 section. P3 fits. (b) The `fix_boundary` is wrong about where to edit. The workflow header (changelog-lint.yml:5-10) states the script is a deployed copy of github-spine/changelog_guard/changelog_duplicate_bullets.py, pushed by Uprava/tools/cologne_batch_deploy.py, with an explicit "edit it there and re-run the deploy; do not fork it per repo". Patching `main()` in this repo's scripts/ would be overwritten on the next deploy and would fork an org-wide guard shared across ~79 repos. The correct fixes are either upstream in github-spine (make the root-vs-recursive behaviour a flag or default) or, repo-locally, extra `- run:` steps in changelog-lint.yml pointing the existing script at each subdirectory — the opposite of the finding's "No change needed in the workflow." One minor detail also worth noting: on this Windows box the root file resolves as `CHANGELOG.md` (case-insensitive `os.path.isfile`) while Linux CI matches `CHANGELOG.md`; the checked file is the same, so this does not affect the finding.

findings.title: Launch-ledger CI gate cannot match a 4-digit handoff ID, so it can no longer flag any missing launch-failure entry
findings.invariant: `--since` must flag every RUN_LOG launch heading whose handoff has no ledger entry; the handoff-ID pattern must match the IDs actually in use.
findings.failure_scenario: `HANDOFF_RE = re.compile(r'\bH\d{3}\b')` matches exactly three digits with a word boundary on both sides, so 'H2889' and 'H1210' do not match (verified: `re.findall(r'\bH\d{3}\b', 'H858 and H2889 and H1210')` -> `['H858']`). Corroborating: the file it scans, src/pilot/RUN_LOG.md, has no heading past 2026-07-13 (last `##` at line 941) — five weeks before the review commit — so the gate has been inert in practice as well as in principle.
findings.evidence: check_launch_ledger.py:28 `HANDOFF_RE = re.compile(r'\bH\d{3}\b')`; :162-164 `handoffs = HANDOFF_RE.findall(title)` / `if handoffs:`. Run: `python src/pilot/check_launch_ledger.py --since 2026-07-05` -> `LAUNCH FAILURE LEDGER: 19 entries complete`, exit 0. `grep -coE 'H[0-9]{4}' src/pilot/RUN_LOG.md` -> 7 (present in the file, none reachable by the gate).

findings.fix_boundary: RussianTranslation/src/pilot/check_launch_ledger.py:28 — widen to `r'\bH\d{3,5}\b'`; add a fixture RUN_LOG with a 4-digit heading and no ledger entry as a negative control.

(1) The corroboration "src/pilot/RUN_LOG.md has no heading past 2026-07-13 (last `##` at line 941), so the gate has been inert in practice" is FALSE — the file is reverse-chronological at the head: line 7 is `## 2026-08-10 — H2533 (Codex) …` and line 20 is `## 2026-07-18 — H1209 …`. The file is live; that strengthens rather than supports the finding. (2) The claim "Every handoff since H1000 is invisible to this gate" is true only of the `--since` sweep; `--handoff H2889` compares `e.get('handoff') == handoff` by string equality and is unaffected, so the documented per-handoff closeout check still sees 4-digit IDs. Additionally, on the real RUN_LOG today widening the regex changes nothing — both existing 4-digit headings are already excluded by the keyword-token filter at :160 ('run'/'aborted'/'workflow'/'max'/'api'/'promoted'), so the defect is a latent false-negative capability, not a currently-realized missed violation. Hence P3, not P2.

findings.title: Dependabot auto-merge falls back to an unconditional squash-merge that bypasses every check
findings.invariant: A dependency bump reaches the default branch only after the repo's checks have passed.
findings.failure_scenario: `gh pr merge --auto --squash "$PR_URL" || gh pr merge --squash "$PR_URL"` — the fallback runs on ANY failure of the first command, not only the intended 'this repo has no required checks' case. `--auto` also fails when auto-merge is disabled at the repository/org level, when the PR is in a state gh rejects, or on a transient API error; in every one of those cases the fallback merges the bump immediately, before CI has run, with `contents: write`. The prior step (:29) is `gh pr review --approve "$PR_URL" || true`, so an approval failure is likewise invisible. Concretely: Dependabot opens a bump of a package used by the runtime lane, auto-merge is off on the repo, the fallback squash-merges it onto master, and the RussianTranslation gates lane goes red only after the change has already landed.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml:34-35 `- name: Enable auto-merge (falls back to a direct squash-merge where no required checks exist)\n  run: gh pr merge --auto --squash "$PR_URL" || gh pr merge --squash "$PR_URL"`; :12-13 `permissions:\n  contents: write`; :29 `run: gh pr review --approve "$PR_URL" || true`.
findings.existing_test_gap: Workflow logic is never exercised — yaml-lint (ci.yml:39-60) only checks that the YAML parses. There is no test or policy check asserting that a merge path is reachable only after checks pass, so the distinction between 'no required checks configured' and 'the --auto call failed' is untested.
findings.fix_boundary: .github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml — drop the `||` fallback, or gate it on an explicit probe that the repo genuinely has no required checks (and on `steps.meta.outputs.update-type != 'version-update:semver-major'` as the header already suggests).

corrections: The defect is not the `||` fallback on line 35. It is (a) master has NO required status checks configured (classic protection lacks required_status_checks; rulesets empty), so BOTH branches of line 35 merge before CI — dropping the fallback fixes nothing; and (b) the semver-major gate the workflow's own header recommends (steps.meta.outputs.update-type != 'version-update:semver-major') is not wired, which is how a major openai bump (>=1.55,<2 -> >=3,<4) squash-merged onto master 18 s after opening in PR #1773. Also strike "bypasses every check": `gh pr merge --squash` cannot bypass branch-protection required checks (the REST merge returns 405); it only bypasses checks that were never made required. Correct fix boundary: add the required-status-check configuration on master and/or the semver-major condition, not the `||` removal.

findings.title: Monthly Cologne-drift alert can never open its first issue: an empty gh --jq lookup returns the string "null"
findings.invariant: When the watcher flags stale promoted rows, an issue must be opened (or an existing one commented) — the alert is the only human-facing output of this scheduled job.
findings.failure_scenario: `NUM=$(gh issue list --search "$TITLE in:title" --state open --json number --jq '.[0].number')`. With no matching issue the JSON array is empty, `.[0].number` evaluates to null, and gh prints the literal `null`. `[ -n "$NUM" ]` is then TRUE (a 4-character string), so the workflow takes the comment branch and runs `gh issue comment null --body "$BODY"`, which fails; the create branch at :78 is unreachable on the first drift month. Result: the very first month that flags stale rows produces a red workflow and no issue, and because the state commit at :49-60 has already run, the next month's incremental diff starts from the new baseline and no longer reports those rows — the drift alert is lost, not merely delayed.
findings.evidence:
.github/workflows/upstream-watch.yml:74-79 `NUM=$(gh issue list --search "$TITLE in:title" --state open --json number --jq '.[0].number')`
`if [ -n "$NUM" ]; then`
`  gh issue comment "$NUM" --body "$BODY"`
`else`
`  gh issue create --title "$TITLE" ...`. The title embeds the month (:72 `TITLE="pwg_ru monthly upstream drift — ${MONTH}"`), so a match is impossible on the first run of any month.
findings.existing_test_gap: The job is schedule-only (:12-13, `cron: 0 7 1 * *`) and its script is inline shell — no test, no dry run, and yaml-lint only proves the file parses. The alert path has never been executed against an empty issue list in CI.
findings.fix_boundary: .github/workflows/upstream-watch.yml:74 — use `--jq '.[0].number // empty'`, or test with `[ -n "$NUM" ] && [ "$NUM" != null ]`.

corrections: The behavioural claim is wrong, not merely mis-located: gh's `--jq` emits an empty string for a null scalar (`jsonScalarToString`, `case nil: return "", nil`), never the 4-character token `null`. `[ -n "$NUM" ]` is therefore FALSE on the first drift month and `gh issue create` at :78 runs as intended. The suggested fix (`// empty`) is a harmless defensive nicety, not a bug fix. The only residual worth keeping is the `existing_test_gap` observation — the alert path is inline shell with no dry run — but that is a hygiene note, not a P2 alert-loss defect.

findings.title: Census counters bypass the exactly-once dedup they are documented to obey, so a re-appended event inflates cards/clean/calls
findings.invariant: Stated at :113 — 'a crash/restart can re-append an event to the append-only log', so every derived count must be exactly-once. The dedup is applied to latency and classification only.
findings.failure_scenario: `build_census` deduplicates `model_call` events by `call_id` for the latency/classification census (:142-151), but the aggregate counters at :161-166 iterate raw `rows`: `calls = sum(int(r.get('calls') or 0) for r in rows)`, `retries` likewise, and `clean`/`cards`/`fidelity` sum every `run_summary` row. A worker that crashes after writing its `run_summary` and is restarted (exactly the scenario :113 names) re-appends that row; the census then reports double the cards, double the clean count, and double the calls — the numbers that feed cost and acceptance reporting. `repeated_by_key` (:155-157, :173) is worse: it scans ALL rows including duplicates and flags a key as a repeated failure at `sum(v.values()) > 1`, so one failure event re-appended once is reported as a recurring per-key defect that never happened.
findings.evidence: run_observability.py:113 `# D-I exactly-once accounting. A crash/restart can re-append an event to the append-only log,`; :161-166 `calls = sum(int(r.get('calls') or 0) for r in rows)` / `retries = sum(...) for r in rows)` / `clean = sum(... for r in rows if r.get('event') == 'run_summary')` — none consult `seen_calls`; :155 `for row in rows:  # by_key scans ALL rows`.
findings.existing_test_gap: run_observability_selftest.py (42 lines) writes each event exactly once — one `run_summary` at :22-24 with cards=2/clean=1/calls=2 — and then asserts `census['calls'] == 2` (:37) and `repeated_by_key['k1'] == {'timeout': 2}` (:27). There is no duplicate-append case anywhere, so the one failure mode the dedup was written for is untested for every counter except latency.
findings.fix_boundary: RussianTranslation/src/pilot/run_observability.py build_census — derive all aggregate counters from the deduped `census_rows` (or key run_summary rows on run_id and dedup them the way call rows are), and add a re-append case to run_observability_selftest.py.

corrections: Three corrections. (1) The invariant is paraphrased too strongly: the :113 comment scopes exactly-once to "call-level 'model_call' events are DEDUPED by call_id" — it never claims every derived count is exactly-once. The defect is the internal inconsistency (`model_calls` deduped, `calls` not), which is what the repo's own C-24 says. (2) "the numbers that feed cost and acceptance reporting" is wrong: the acceptance GO verdict is computed from `outputs` and written before `write_census`, and cost comes from `economy_ledger.py` which dedups on `run_id` and documents at :13 that its numerator is explicitly NOT the census `calls` counter. Nothing programmatic reads the census. (3) The finding under-reports: `classification_counts` is also inflated, because run_summary rows fall through to `census_rows.append(r)` at :152 with no dedup — so the "classification census is protected by the dedup" premise is itself false for non-model_call events. Also: not novel — C-24 in H963 (16-07-2026) and H1110 (17-07-2026, "🔴 open").

findings.title: RUN_FREQ_MAX.md states 300 000 ms is the absolute per-call maximum and that --timeout defaults to 300; the code's ceiling and default are both 600 000 ms / 600 s
findings.invariant: The runbook's 'Current operating truth' must state the ceiling the code actually enforces; an operator sizing a window or pasting a canary command from it is choosing spend against that number.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator follows the canary recipe the doc says to paste (RUN_FREQ_MAX.md:727-729: `--only-profile c4 --max-agents 1 --timeout 300 …`) believing 300 s is the enforced maximum. Per the doc's own #983 note at :743-746 a `--timeout` value only ever LOWERS the effective bound, so the canary runs against 300 000 ms — a ceiling H2313's own measurement placed below the completed-spawn p95 (342 997 ms, p90 = 276 521 ms). Healthy slow spawns are killed, and the operator reads the kill as a route/health failure because the doc told them 300 000 was the ceiling everyone else runs at.

findings.existing_test_gap: execution_contract_selftest.py and headless_worker_selftest.test_kill_ceiling_in_step_with_harness pin the constant's consistency across code paths, but no check compares the constant to the prose in RUN_FREQ_MAX.md, so the doc can drift a full 2x without any CI signal.

findings.title: DATA_LICENSE.md says CITATION.cff stays at 'version: unreleased' until the edition cut is archived and a DOI registered; the committed CITATION.cff carries version 1.144.36 with a release date and no DOI
findings.invariant: The licence file's statement about the machine-readable citation metadata must match that file; a citation-manager consumer resolves CITATION.cff, not the prose that describes it.
findings.failure_scenario: A third party cites the dataset via GitHub's 'Cite this repository' widget (which reads CITATION.cff) and gets 'pwg_ru … version 1.144.36, released 2026-08-12' — a formally released, numbered, DOI-less edition. The precondition DATA_LICENSE.md names (immutable edition cut archived + DOI registered, DOI_PLAN.md:5-9) has not happened; G10_immutable_edition_cut is still `partial` in roadmap/quality_gates.jsonl. Nobody can later resolve or correct that citation because no DOI anchors it.
findings.affected: external citers; DOI/release posture
findings.evidence: DOC — DATA_LICENSE.md:51-54: 'A machine-readable [CITATION.cff](…) sits beside this file and declares the same `CC-BY-SA-4.0` licence. It stays at `version: unreleased` until the immutable edition cut is archived and a DOI is registered against it — see [DOI_PLAN.md](…).' ARTIFACT — RussianTranslation/CITATION.cff:19-20: `version: 1.144.36` / `date-released: 2026-08-12`, and the file has no `doi:` or `identifiers:` key at all. DOI_PLAN.md:9 still lists as a pending step 'Register the DOI against that immutable directory and update `CITATION.cff` with the DOI and final version.' roadmap/quality_gates.jsonl: `G10_immutable_edition_cut | partial | blocks_print=True`.

corrections: Two corrections. (1) The failure scenario is wrong: GitHub's "Cite this repository" widget resolves only a root (or .github/ or docs/) CITATION.cff, and this repo has one — /CITATION.cff, `version: 1.144.75`, `date-released: 2026-08-17`, with a deliberate concept `doi: 10.5281/zenodo.21306715`. A third-party citer using the widget therefore gets the MIT software citation with a resolvable DOI, never "pwg_ru … 1.144.36, DOI-less". The exposed surface is only someone who navigates into RussianTranslation/ and reads the subdirectory file directly, or a downstream cff-parser pointed at that path — real, but far narrower than "external citers" generally. Hence P3, not P2. (2) The fix_boundary is too narrow: the same "version is/stays `unreleased`" claim is repeated in RussianTranslation/METHODOLOGY_REVIEW.md:147 and RussianTranslation/PRINT_DH_SPEED_REVIEW.md:52, so fixing DATA_LICENSE.md:52-54 alone still leaves two stale assertions. Root cause worth naming in the fix: the org /cut-release ritual mechanically syncs every CITATION.cff's version+date-released (git history shows 1.74.0 → 1.144.22 → 1.144.32 → 1.144.33 → 1.144.36 in `chore(release)` commits), so "stays at unreleased" was never an enforceable posture for a file inside a repo that cuts releases — the prose is what should change, not the artifact.

findings.title: watch_upstream never routes `removed` headwords to the stale worklist, and advances layer state past them — a latent notification gap, with no observed trigger in the whole upstream history
findings.invariant: The watcher's stated contract (watch_upstream.py:5-8) is that any upstream change to a headword we already translated must reach `<YYYY-MM>.stale.json`, the machine worklist the drain consumes. State may only advance past a change that was emitted.
findings.failure_scenario: Cologne deletes or renames a PWG headword we have promoted (a rename appears as removed+added under a different form_key, and csl-orig actively edits keys — that is why input_raw_sha256 exists). `changed_headwords` returns it in `removed` (line 107), but line 276 feeds only `changed | added` into `_stale_for`, so no stale entry is produced. `_render_md` prints "No promoted rows affected." (line 223) and the headline "0 promoted row-group(s) flagged stale this month" (line 192). Line 281 then unconditionally sets `state['cologne'][code] = head`, so the next month's run diffs from the new HEAD and the deletion is permanently unrecoverable. The store keeps serving a Russian translation of an entry that no longer exists upstream, and no future run can ever discover it. The per-layer table does print a `removed` count (line 209), so the human report and the machine worklist actively disagree.
findings.affected: Any promoted row whose upstream csl-orig record is deleted or whose key1 is corrected upstream; and every layer, permanently, if a layer file is ever renamed at HEAD.
findings.evidence:
watch_upstream.py:275-281 —
        changed, added, removed = changed_headwords(old_text, new_text)
        stale = _stale_for(changed | added, code, promoted)
        all_stale.extend(stale)
        per_layer[code] = {'changed': len(changed), 'added': len(added),
                           'removed': len(removed),
                           'flagged_rows': sum(len(s['lines']) for s in stale)}
        state['cologne'][code] = head
The same shape hides a second failure: `show_file` returns None on ANY non-zero git exit (line 71), so if `v02/<code>/<code>.txt` is renamed or removed at HEAD, `index_text(None)` returns {} (line 81-82) → changed=added=∅, removed=everything → an empty worklist, a clean-looking report, and state advanced.
findings.existing_test_gap: `selftest()` at watch_upstream.py:414-459 asserts `changed_headwords` computes `removed` correctly (line 425) but never asserts that a removed key reaches `_stale_for` or the worklist — it only exercises `_stale_for` with a changed key (line 432). The assertion stops one call short of the defect.
findings.fix_boundary: watch_upstream.run_cologne lines 273-281: which of (changed, added, removed) route to the worklist, and the precondition for advancing `state['cologne'][code]` (must not advance when `new_text is None`, and must not advance past unemitted removals).

corrections: What survives is much narrower and is a notification gap, not a correctness defect: in a hypothetical month where the ONLY drift is a key rename (removed X + added Y, our promoted row under X), the worklist stays empty, so .github/workflows/upstream-watch.yml's "Open / update drift issue" step exits early on `STALE -eq 0` and nobody is pinged — the evidence lands only as nonzero `added`/`removed` cells in the committed `<YYYY-MM>.md`. Not "permanently unrecoverable" (the sha pair is committed in `_state.json` history and in each month's `csl_orig_head`), not "a clean-looking report" (the removed count is printed to both the md table and stdout), and not observed even once in the available csl-orig history. The cheap real fix is to gate the CI issue on `stale or any(per_layer[*]['removed'] or per_layer[*]['added'])` rather than on `len(stale)` alone; changing `_stale_for(changed | added)` to include `removed` would be wrong, since the drain lane it feeds is defined as re-translation and a deleted headword has no input to regenerate.

Three corrections. (1) "Permanently unrecoverable / no future run can ever discover it" is overstated: `_state.json` is tracked in git (verified `git ls-files --error-unmatch`) and csl-orig retains history, so a human can restore the old sha and re-diff; the committed `<YYYY-MM>.md` also keeps the `removed=N` count forever. (2) The finding *understates* the concealment in the opposite direction: the CI step "Open / update drift issue when rows are flagged" computes STALE from `stale.json` and exits 0 when it is zero, so a month whose only upstream change is a removal of a promoted headword opens no issue at all — the human report with the `removed` count is committed but never surfaced. (3) The `new_text is None` variant is not silent in the table (my fixture printed `removed=2`, i.e. the whole layer), only in the worklist and headline; and `removed` cannot literally be routed into the existing worklist, since a deleted headword has nothing to re-translate — the correct fix is a separate orphan bucket plus refusing to advance `state['cologne'][code]` when `new_text is None` or when removals touched promoted rows. Severity P2 rather than P1: reachable, silent and contract-breaking, but latent (zero occurrences in the 4 relevant layers in the observed 2-month window), bounded to the 254 promoted form_keys, and recoverable from git-tracked state.

findings.lead_adjudication: Both lenses are right about different things, so neither verdict is taken whole. Reproduction CONFIRMED the mechanism by driving the real `run_cologne` against a temp csl-orig fixture: a deleted promoted record yields `removed=1`, `stale: []`, a report headline reading '0 promoted row-group(s) flagged stale', and state advanced. Correctness REFUTED the premise: re-running the watcher's own `changed_headwords` over the entire available csl-orig history for all four layers (pwg 37 commits, pw 4, sch 3, pwkvn 2, back to 14-06-2026) gives added=0 and removed=0 EVERYWHERE — including the 105,696-record 'PWG fully copied from v1e of AB' rewrite, which preserved every single form_key. The reporter's stated premise, that csl-orig actively edits keys, is measurably false over the observed period. Ruling: keep the finding, drop the claim that it has happened or is likely, and drop 'permanently unrecoverable' (`_state.json` is tracked in git and csl-orig retains history, so a human can rewind). P1 -> P3 latent. It is worth keeping only because the failure would be silent: the human table prints a `removed` count while the machine worklist does not, so the two surfaces disagree by construction.

findings.title: prompt_compiler.selftest() rewrites its own committed goldens before comparing them, so the golden half of the test can never fail — the compiler-vs-builder oracle is what actually guards prompt assembly
findings.invariant: The committed fixtures under src/pilot/fixtures/pwg_cache_economy/ are FROZEN expectations: `reconstruct_legacy_claude`/`reconstruct_legacy_deepseek` exist to prove that today's live prompt builders (headless_worker.prompt_blocks, deepseek_arm.SYSTEM_TMPL, prep_pack.flash_messages) still emit the same bytes and the same cache `request_id` as when the fixture was frozen. Next `pytest tests/test_pwg_cache_economy.py` runs `test_compiler_golden_bytes` -> `prompt_compiler.selftest()` -> line 343 `write_golden_fixtures(FIXTURE_DIR)`, which at line 336 opens both tracked goldens with mode 'w' and overwrites them from the NEW builders. Lines 344-351 then load those just-written files and compare them against the same builders. The assertions 'Claude legacy reconstruction drifted' (:252) and 'Claude request id drifted from golden' (:349) compare the new output to itself and always pass. The suite reports PASS, the tracked fixtures silently change under git, and the cache `request_id` namespace rebases with no gate ever firing.
findings.affected: Every cached/compiled request identity in the pwg_ru cache economy (cache_generation_pairs, cache_prep_pairs, cache_migrate all import prompt_compiler), plus the two tracked golden fixtures which are silently mutated on every test run.
findings.evidence: prompt_compiler.py:341-351 — `def selftest():` / `    os.makedirs(FIXTURE_DIR, exist_ok=True)` / `    write_golden_fixtures(FIXTURE_DIR)` / `    claude = load_json('legacy_claude_prompt.json')` / `    deep = load_json('legacy_deepseek_payload.json')` / `    rec_c = reconstruct_legacy_claude(claude)` ... `raise AssertionError('Claude request id drifted from golden')`. It cannot catch drift because the function it calls rewrites the comparison baseline on its first statement. tests/test_pwg_cache_prep_h2704.py:99 makes the identical call. No test asserts the fixture files are unchanged after the run, and there is no CI step that fails on a dirty working tree, so the rewrite is invisible.
findings.fix_boundary: prompt_compiler.py:341-343 — delete the `write_golden_fixtures(FIXTURE_DIR)` call from `selftest()`; golden regeneration is already reachable and deliberate via `--write-goldens` (prompt_compiler.py:389-392). corrections: Three corrections. (1) Wrong trigger examples: neither `MASK_PREAMBLE` (gen_opt_harness2.py:715) nor `prep_pack.PREP_FLASH_SYSTEM` can reach a golden fixture. `write_golden_fixtures` hardcodes a synthetic manifest (`'preamble': 'PREAMBLE\n'`) and prompt_compiler never imports gen_opt_harness2, so a MASK_PREAMBLE edit changes nothing in the fixture; and there is no PREP golden at all — prompt_compiler.py:378-386 compares `compile_prep_flash_v0` against live `prep_pack.flash_messages`, a pure self-consistency check that a frozen fixture would not fix either. The real triggers I verified are `headless_worker.card_block`/`prompt_blocks`, `deepseek_arm.SYSTEM_TMPL`, and `cache_identity.COMPILER_VERSION`/`build_request_record`. (2) Incomplete fix boundary: deleting prompt_compiler.py:343 alone does not close it — `cache_migrate.py:251` calls `compiler.write_golden_fixtures()` unconditionally inside its own `selftest()`, which `tests/test_pwg_cache_economy.py:30 test_migrate_round_trip_and_refusal` runs in the same `pytest tests -q`. Both sites must go. (3) Blast radius inflated: "every cached/compiled request identity" overstates it. Dropping the antecedent manufactures the invariant. (2) The invariant that matters IS enforced, fixture-independently: the same selftest asserts compiler bytes == headless_worker.build_prompt and == prep_pack.flash_messages, plus the two identity mutations (a model change must move the request_id; path/run extras must not). Ruling: CONFIRMED as a dead assertion, P1 -> P3. Fix is one line — drop the write_golden_fixtures call from selftest() and leave it to --write-goldens, which already exists.

findings.title: The Lane-C CI card gate's wf_output scope (`gatelogs/`) does not match where the coordinator writes wf_output — a latent scope bug in an unwired Wave-2 stub
findings.invariant: Every added/modified workflow result in a pwg-ru-data PR must pass the deterministic store-corruption checks (non-empty `russian` on every sense, zero `{Tn}` residue, zero SAN-LOSS/UNMAPPED) before the `gates-green` label authorises auto-merge (module docstring rule 2; ARCHITECTURE §'Lane C: gated PR → CI → auto-merge').
findings.failure_scenario: A Lane-C PR adds `manifests/coordinator/artifacts/<lease>/wf_output.<lease>.json` containing a card with `russian: ""` and unrestored `{T3}` residue, plus a `tm/**` row and any file under `telemetry/`. `run_gates` computes `wf_payloads = [f for f in files if f.startswith('gatelogs/') ...]` → `[]`, so `check_wf_payload` is never called on a single file; the only surviving rule (`tm_changes and not telemetry_changes`) is satisfied. `main()` prints `✓ gates green` and returns 0, the workflow applies `gates-green`, and the corrupt window auto-merges into the data repo.

No test cross-checks `run_gates`'s prefix against `coordinator.paths()['artifacts']`, `data_root.ENV_LAYOUT`, or `data_inventory`'s migration table, which is exactly where the disagreement lives.
findings.fix_boundary: `ci_gate_runner.run_gates` — derive the wf_output scope from the same layout table the pipeline writes through (a `**/wf_output*.json` match anywhere in the diff, or a constant shared with `data_root`/`coordinator.ARTIFACT_DIRNAME`) instead of the literal `'gatelogs/'` prefix; and fail closed when a PR touches `tm/**` with zero matched wf_output payloads.

corrections: Three corrections. (1) Blast radius: "the corrupt window auto-merges into the data repo" is not reachable — pwg-ru-data has no auto-merge workflow (only gates.yml), has never had a PR, and gates.yml has never run; the label is consumed by Wave 2, which is unbuilt. (2) Reachability: no producer emits a Lane-C PR at all — cloud_window.run_cloud_window has zero non-selftest callers and declares itself unscheduled in Wave 1, so the "disagreement between run_gates and the producers" has never been exercised in either direction. Note the gate's card branch is equally inert today: since nothing writes `gatelogs/wf_output*`, check_wf_payload has never scanned a real file either. (3) Fix direction is not settled: the module docstring rule 3 states a PR "may stage cards in `gatelogs/`", and gates.yml's own paths filter excludes `manifests/**`, so making the Lane-C producer stage into gatelogs/ is as defensible as widening run_gates' glob — the finding presents one side as the proven-correct constant when the convention was simply never wired. Severity should be P3 (latent defect in a pre-go-live stub the repo already flags as end-to-end untested), not P0; it must be fixed before Lane C is enabled, but nothing is currently unguarded by it.

findings.title: BoundedSupervisor's terminal checkpoint records a consumed-but-uncompleted window as neither completed nor pending — an accounting slip, not a dropped unit
findings.invariant: A window pulled from the plan queue or requeue backlog is either recorded in `completed_window_ids` or left restorable in the persisted checkpoint — the loop never checkpoints a state in which an item has been consumed from both the backlog/`next_index` and from `completed_window_ids` (the same silent-loss class the module fails loudly on at lines 341-348 and 353-360).
findings.failure_scenario: A bounded run has `--cost-ceiling` set (so `budget_cap is not None` and `usage_counter` is wired by bounded_staged_run.build_supervisor:876-881). `_pull()` pops requeue item `rq-001-w04` off `requeue_backlog` (line 269). `make_run_window`'s drain raises `SystemExit('… has 1 failed job(s) …')` (bounded_staged_run.py:643). The `except BaseException` handler re-syncs the ledger, sees `cost_evaluable` false, calls `_finish(STOP_COST_UNEVALUABLE)` → `_write_checkpoint()`, and breaks. The written checkpoint has `requeue_backlog` WITHOUT `rq-001-w04` and `completed_window_ids` without it either. `--resume` restores that checkpoint (`_load_checkpoint` lines 588-590), `_pull()` finds nothing for those keys, and the loop terminates with `STOP_CLEAN_TARGET` reporting success. The rejected headwords are never re-translated and nothing says so. Identical for a plan window: `_pull()` already did `self.next_index += 1` at line 275 before returning it.
findings.evidence:
bounded_supervisor.py:268-278 `item = self.requeue_backlog.pop(0)` / `self.next_index += 1` — both consume before returning. bounded_supervisor.py:322-333: `try: wf_output = self.run_window(item)
 except BaseException:
     self._sync_call_counter(); self._sync_usage_counter()
     if self.budget_cap is not None and not self._durable_cost_evaluable:
         self._finish(STOP_COST_UNEVALUABLE)
         break
     raise`. `_finish` (line 456-458) calls `_write_checkpoint()`, and `_state_dict` (lines 540-556) persists `requeue_backlog`, `next_index` and `completed_window_ids` — the item is in none of them. The bare `raise` path is safe by contrast: no checkpoint is written, so the previous iteration's checkpoint still holds the item.
findings.existing_test_gap: `bounded_supervisor_selftest.test_p_durable_cost_counter` (lines 511-517) exercises exactly this branch — `def crashed(_window): usage['cost_evaluable'] = False; raise RuntimeError(...)` — but asserts only `sup.run()['stop_reason'] == STOP_COST_UNEVALUABLE`. It never opens the checkpoint, and its plan is a single window `[{'id': 'crash'}]`, so a dropped item is indistinguishable from a drained queue. `test_f_crash_recovery` (lines 183-219) DOES assert `state['next_index'] == 2` after a crash, but only on the `raise` path (no `budget_cap`), so it validates the safe branch and leaves the lossy one uncovered.
findings.fix_boundary: `BoundedSupervisor.run`'s `except BaseException` handler — push the consumed item back (`self.requeue_backlog.insert(0, item)` or `self.next_index -= 1`) before `_finish(STOP_COST_UNEVALUABLE)`, or move the consume out of `_pull` into the post-audit commit alongside `completed_window_ids.append`.

corrections: Two corrections. (a) The consumed item is NOT dropped on --resume: the same checkpoint carries stop_reason='cost_unevaluable', and BoundedSupervisor.run() returns immediately on a restored stop_reason (bounded_supervisor.py:290-291), so the resumed run re-reports cost_unevaluable with windows_done unchanged and exit code 1 — never STOP_CLEAN_TARGET, never a success claim. The selftest encodes this contract at bounded_supervisor_selftest.py:204 (a resumable checkpoint must have stop_reason None). (b) Independently, CallReservationLedger.usage()['cost_evaluable'] is a per-run monotone latch (call_reservation.py:471-475; unevaluable_calls is never decremented) and --resume is bound to an existing run_id (bounded_staged_run.py:951-963), so the top-of-loop gate at bounded_supervisor.py:299 would re-fire even if stop_reason were cleared. The real residue is cosmetic and P3 at most: the terminal checkpoint's next_index over-reads by one relative to completed_window_ids/windows_done. It costs nothing because the checkpoint is never used to continue after a _finish, a fresh non-resume run re-offers every window, the sqlite 'failed' job row persists, and the requeued keys remain in the checkpoint's own history entry.

The state-loss half is real and I reproduced it byte-for-byte; the CONSEQUENCE half of the failure_scenario is wrong. `--resume` does NOT "terminate with STOP_CLEAN_TARGET reporting success". `_state_dict` persists `'stop_reason'` (bounded_supervisor.py:553) and `_load_checkpoint` restores it (:596), and `run()` opens with `if self.stop_reason: return self.summary()` (:290-291). So a resumed supervisor whose checkpoint carries `cost_unevaluable` is a hard no-op: it runs zero windows and re-reports `stop_reason=cost_unevaluable`, which `bounded_staged_run.py:1025` maps to exit 1. Measured: RUN1 `stop=cost_unevaluable`, checkpoint `next_index=2 completed=['w0'] backlog=[] stop=cost_unevaluable`; RESUME `stop=cost_unevaluable ran=[] windows_done=1`. The scenario's silent `clean_target` only appears after hand-editing `stop_reason` to null in the checkpoint JSON (my repro2: AFTER-SURGERY `stop=clean_target ran=[] requeue_backlog_len=0`) — nothing in the codebase clears `stop_reason` (grepped every assignment in src/pilot). Second correction: "the rejected headwords are never re-translated" overstates it. A window whose audit produced `requeue_keys` fails `_audit_is_clean`, so it is never promoted (bounded_staged_run.py audit closure), and `no_pwg_scale_plan.py` "skips headwords already present in the translated store" (:8, :47, `read_store_keys`) — a regenerated plan re-offers exactly those keys. The real residue is therefore a permanently wedged checkpoint (loud, exit 1) plus a lost audit trail of which item was consumed, not a silent data loss. Severity P1 -> P3; the one-line fix in fix_boundary is still correct and worth taking.

findings.lead_adjudication: The two lenses split cleanly between mechanism and consequence, and the consequence is the half that was claimed. Both verifiers reproduced the lossy write: under a cost ceiling, a `run_window` crash with `cost_evaluable` false checkpoints `next_index=2` with `completed_window_ids=['w1']` and w2 in neither list. Correctness then REFUTED the stated harm, mechanically: the same `_finish` call persists `stop_reason='cost_unevaluable'` before writing (bounded_supervisor.py:458-459), `_load_checkpoint` restores it (:596), and `run()` opens with `if self.stop_reason: return self.summary()` (:290-291) — so that checkpoint is TERMINAL, not a resume point, and `--resume` cannot 'terminate with STOP_CLEAN_TARGET reporting success'. The module's own `test_f_crash_recovery` asserts exactly this contract. Ruling: the write really does lose the window's status, so a human reading the checkpoint cannot tell whether w2 ran; but nothing is silently dropped and no run falsely reports success. P1 -> P3, retitled to the accounting slip.

findings.title: Every coordinator subprocess on the unattended drain path runs with no timeout — the nonstop loop has no watchdog against a wedged child
findings.invariant: An unattended loop bounds every child it spawns. The per-call model spawn is bounded (`run_tree_kill(..., timeout=wrapper_timeout_s(timeout))`, max_account_orchestrator.py:517) and the coordinator bounds its own audit child (`AUDIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, coordinator.py:1591), but the orchestration calls that sit on the same critical path are unbounded.
findings.failure_scenario: `bounded_staged_run --execute` runs unattended (Task Scheduler tick, ARCHITECTURE §Lane A). Its per-lease drain calls `mao.cmd_record_done`, which calls `coordinator_command(args, ['record-output', …])`. That child runs `promote_final_cards`/`translation_memory` work whose TM rebuild the codebase itself documents as legitimately exceeding 10 minutes (coordinator.py:167-170, A1/H1283). If that child wedges — a stuck fsync on the store, a network-mounted data root, a rebuild that never terminates — `subprocess.run` blocks forever with no timeout. The parent's own guards (`drain_no_progress_passes`, `max_drain_iterations`, `STAGED_RUN_IDLE_POLL_SECONDS`) all sit in the loop body and never get another turn, so the lane stalls silently and indefinitely with a coordinator lease still in `in_progress`.
findings.evidence: max_account_orchestrator.py:189-192 `proc = subprocess.run(\n        [sys.executable, coordinator] + list(command),\n        cwd=..., env=env, text=True, encoding='utf-8', capture_output=True)` — no `timeout=`. The same shape repeats on the live drain path: bounded_staged_run.py:719-723 (in-loop `promote-ready`), 735-739 (post-loop rescue `promote-ready`), 467 (`auto_promote_window`), and 536 `run = run or subprocess.run` in `materialize_requeue`. coordinator.py:560-562 `run_cmd` likewise defaults `timeout=None`. execution_contract.py:88-89 already names the missing watchdog for the model call ('Separating "hung" from "very slow" for real needs a no-output-progress watchdog … left as residual work'); the subprocess half is not acknowledged anywhere.
findings.existing_test_gap: `max_account_orchestrator_selftest.py` and `bounded_staged_run_selftest.py` both inject fake/fixture runners for the coordinator step (bounded_staged_run.py:533-536 documents `run` as 'injectable for the hermetic selftest'), so no test ever runs a real coordinator child, let alone a hanging one. There is no test that asserts a `timeout=` is passed to any orchestration subprocess, so the omission is structurally invisible to the suite.
findings.fix_boundary: `max_account_orchestrator.coordinator_command` and the four `subprocess.run` sites in `bounded_staged_run` (`auto_promote_window`, the in-loop promote, the rescue promote, `materialize_requeue`) — pass an explicit bound derived from `coordinator.AUDIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`/a new promotion ceiling and classify the expiry as a loud stop, not a silent block.

corrections: Substance is wrong, not just detail: the unattended loop DOES bound its child. Any surviving version of this finding must be restated as (a) the inner subprocesses are unbounded, so a wedge is only caught by the outer 4 h window timeout rather than promptly, and (b) `subprocess.run`'s timeout kills only `bounded_staged_run`, leaving a wedged coordinator grandchild orphaned and its lease stuck in `in_progress` — a P3 cleanup issue, not a silent-indefinite-stall. The evidence line "the nonstop loop has no watchdog" should be struck; nonstop_scheduler.py:211-212 + 327-330 is that watchdog, built deliberately under H2246.

findings.title: economy_ledger.write_ledger reads the import-time FROZEN_LOG, defeating the lazy --data-root seam it documents two lines above
findings.invariant: `$PWG_ECONOMY_LOG` is the `--data-root` seam for this module and must be resolved lazily, so an in-process caller that applies a data root in its own `main()` — after importing this module — reads that root's telemetry (the contract stated at economy_ledger.py:70-74 and implemented by `frozen_log()`).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller does `import economy_ledger as el` at module scope (bounded_staged_run.py:77 already does exactly this), then `data_root.apply(root)` in its `main()` (data_root.py:95-96 `env.update(values)`), then `el.write_ledger(out_path)` with `rows=None`. `FROZEN_LOG` was frozen at import to `src/pilot/generation_api_probe_log.jsonl` (the historical local path), so the ledger is built over the WRONG data root's telemetry and published as the requested root's economy ledger — and `build_ledger`'s `source_log` provenance (line 254) is filled in from the same stale constant, so the artifact names a log it did not read.

findings.existing_test_gap: `economy_ledger_selftest.test_write_ledger_roundtrip` (line 210-214) always passes `rows=` and `source_log=` explicitly (`el.write_ledger(out, rows=rows, source_log='synthetic.jsonl')`), so the `rows is None` branch is never executed. `bounded_staged_run_selftest.py:1298` asserts `el.frozen_log() == os.environ['PWG_ECONOMY_LOG']` — it pins the lazy helper and never touches `write_ledger`, so the one consumer that ignores the helper is uncovered.
findings.fix_boundary: `economy_ledger.write_ledger` (and the `--log` argparse default at line 409, plus `build_ledger`'s `source_log` fallback at line 254) — call `frozen_log()` at use time instead of reading the module constant.

corrections: The finding is right that `write_ledger` reads the eager constant while the module documents a lazy seam, but wrong on impact on two counts. (a) The `rows is None` branch is dead — no caller in the repo invokes `write_ledger` without explicit `rows=`, so no ledger has ever been or can currently be built over the wrong root; this is a latent hazard for future callers, not a live wrong-data path. (b) The `build_ledger` `source_log` fallback at line 254 is `os.path.basename(FROZEN_LOG)`, and data_root.py:48 keeps the filename `generation_api_probe_log.jsonl` under every root, so the provenance string is identical either way — that half of the claim is void outright, and the argparse default at 409 is resolved at process start where the env is already correct. findings.title: G5 print gate is unblocked by one print-ready row — REFUTED: that is the documented criterion, and the finding's scale was fabricated
findings.invariant: The translation-store review gate must express a coverage threshold — some meaningful share of the store reviewed and machine-clean — before the edition cut is declared unblocked.
findings.failure_scenario: review_summary() (lines 63-70) counts every store row for which store_flags.is_print_ready(row) is True (review_status in PRINT_READY_STATUSES AND machine_ok(row) — store_flags.py:75). local_gate_blockers() at line 123 then blocks G5 only when that count is exactly zero. A store of ~1.9M rows with a single human-approved, machine-clean row therefore reports G5 as not-a-blocker; combined with C6-01 the whole upstream_blockers set at edition_summary():136 goes empty and ready_to_cut becomes True. review_state() at line 42 makes the same call and can only ever return 'blocked' or 'partial' — there is no 'ready' state and no denominator: the printed detail 'review decisions %d/%d, print-ready %d' mixes a review-CSV row count with a store row count, two different populations, so a reader cannot even see what fraction of the store is print-ready.
findings.evidence: preflight_remaining_gates.py:123-124 `if review['print_ready_rows'] == 0: blockers.append('G5_translation_store_review_gate')`; :42 `return 'blocked' if s['print_ready_rows'] == 0 else 'partial'`; :44 the detail string pairs s['decisions']/s['rows'] (from REVIEW_CSV, lines 51-62) with s['print_ready_rows'] (from STORE, lines 63-70).
findings.existing_test_gap: No test feeds a one-row-print-ready store and asserts G5 still blocks; the fixture path (--skip-local-human-artifacts, line 215) skips the human artifacts entirely.
findings.fix_boundary: local_gate_blockers / review_state need a ratio against the store's reviewable population (print_ready_rows / eligible_rows) with an explicit floor, and review_summary should report both counts against the same denominator.

corrections: Two factual corrections to the finding: (1) the store is 11,603 rows, not "~1.9M", and it already holds 3 print-ready rows — the hypothetical is the current live state, and G10 is still blocked, which disproves the stated chain; (2) "combined with C6-01 the whole upstream_blockers set goes empty and ready_to_cut becomes True" is wrong — upstream_blockers is a union with roadmap_blockers(), which today contains G5, G6 and G7 from quality_gates.jsonl; no code path writes that file, so only a human registry edit can empty it. What survives is a much smaller, cosmetic point worth at most P3: the review_state()/write_dashboard detail string "review decisions %d/%d, print-ready %d" pairs a REVIEW_CSV denominator with a STORE numerator, so a reader cannot see the print-ready share of the store. That is a display/legibility nit in a report-only dashboard, not a violated gate invariant.

Three claims in the finding are wrong and must be struck. (1) "A store of ~1.9M rows" — the real store is 11,603 rows and the documented review slice is 217 rows; the fabricated scale inflates the severity. (2) "combined with C6-01 the whole upstream_blockers set at edition_summary():136 goes empty and ready_to_cut becomes True" — false as stated: upstream_blockers = (roadmap_blockers() - G10) | gate_blockers, and quality_gates.jsonl still carries G5 status 'partial', so I measured blocked_by = [G5, G6, G7] and ready_to_cut = False on the live tree. Emptying it additionally requires a human to hand-flip G5 to 'passing' in roadmap/quality_gates.jsonl (no automation writes that file). (3) The asserted invariant ("must express a coverage threshold") is not the repo's invariant: roadmap/print_review_minimum.json states done_when = "print-ready rows are nonzero", and release_readiness.py:83 implements the same `== 0` test — so this is a specification/gate-design weakness, not code-vs-intent drift. Minor: the existing_test_gap prose is inaccurate — --skip-local-human-artifacts (line 213) skips only the two subprocess validators (validate_review, gold_status), not review_summary/local_gate_blockers, which do run in CI; CI is immune only because the store is gitignored, so print_ready_rows=0 there. The conclusion (no test pins the aggregate) still holds: tests/test_store_flags.py pins only the per-row predicate. What survives and is worth fixing: review_state():44 and write_dashboard():174-177 print "decisions %d/%d, print-ready %d" pairing an 11,163-row review-CSV denominator with a 3-of-11,603 store count — a human reading "5/11163, print-ready 3" cannot see that 0.026% of the store is print-ready, and that human is the one who decides whether to flip quality_gates.jsonl to 'passing'.

findings.lead_adjudication: Refuted on the decisive ground that the code implements the written contract. HUMAN_REVIEW_MINIMIZATION.md:95 states the G5 exit criterion verbatim — 'Done when: G5 reports review decisions present and at least one print-ready row' — in a document whose stated goal is 'the smallest valid human workload'. Coverage is enforced structurally rather than by a ratio: `export_interop.approved_store` admits only `approved`/`human_reviewed`, so an edition carries exactly the reviewed rows and no inflated claim is possible. Two of the finding's factual claims are also false: the store is 11,603 rows, not '~1.9M', and it already holds 3 print-ready rows, i.e. the hypothetical IS the current live state — and G10 is still blocked, which is the opposite of what the finding predicts. Ruling: REFUTED, preserved. One genuine residual survives at P3: `preflight_remaining_gates.py:44` prints 'review decisions %d/%d, print-ready %d' mixing a review-CSV row count with a store row count — two different populations in one line, so a reader cannot see what fraction of the store is print-ready.

findings.title: The LOD acceptance gate's "no placeholder example.org IRI" invariant only inspects the object position, so a placeholder namespace on entry subjects passes
findings.invariant: An invariant asserting a placeholder namespace is absent from the graph must cover every position an IRI can occupy (subject, predicate, object).
findings.failure_scenario: The check is `SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?n){?s ?p ?o FILTER(isIRI(?o) && CONTAINS(STR(?o),"example.org"))}` — bound to `?o` alone. `ontolex:LexicalEntry` resources appear in the graph overwhelmingly as SUBJECTS (`pwg:X a ontolex:LexicalEntry ; ontolex:sense pwg:X_sense_1`); nothing in the lexical graph points AT an entry. If --base-iri were left at, or regressed to, the placeholder namespace that export_lod's own docstring (lines 5-7) exists to replace (`https://example.org/pwg/ru/` — still the live default in the sibling export_interop.py:154), every entry IRI in the emitted graph would be an example.org IRI and this gate would still report PASS, because those IRIs never appear as an object of any triple. The gate names itself as the defence against exactly that regression and does not provide it.
findings.evidence: lod_acceptance.py:121-122 `ok = check('no placeholder example.org IRI remains',` / `           count(g, 'SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?n){?s ?p ?o FILTER(isIRI(?o) && CONTAINS(STR(?o),"example.org"))}') == 0) and ok`. The placeholder it guards against is still the shipped default one file over: export_interop.py:154 `f.write('@prefix pwg: <https://example.org/pwg/ru/> .\n\n')`.
findings.existing_test_gap: There is no negative test that feeds lod_acceptance a graph built with --base-iri https://example.org/ and asserts the invariant FAILS. Every run of the gate is against the fixture already built with the ruled w3id namespace, so the check has only ever been observed passing on clean input — the condition under which a position-restricted filter and a correct one are indistinguishable.
findings.fix_boundary: lod_acceptance.py test_invariants: replace the single-position filter with a union over ?s, ?p and ?o (or iterate g.all_nodes() plus predicates in Python), and add a negative fixture asserting the check fails on a placeholder-namespace graph.

corrections: The finding's premise is wrong on data, not just on degree. Under a placeholder-base regression the existing object-only filter returns 1,141 non-zero and the gate FAILS — it does provide the defence it names, because the base namespace also carries the vocab classes (rdf:type objects), grade concepts, sense IRIs and vartrans source/target IRIs. The claim "nothing in the lexical graph points AT an entry" is also false (40 vartrans:target triples). The only residue is stylistic: the filter is narrower than the invariant it states, and there is no negative fixture — worth a one-line UNION over ?s/?p/?o for robustness, but no live failure exists.

findings.title: No ExecStart line in the orchestrator unit carries a `-` prefix, so a non-zero `run-once` skips `record-done` for that tick — real in the unit file, but the unit is deployed nowhere
findings.invariant: Harvesting completed, already-paid coordinator output must not be conditional on the dispatch step of the same tick succeeding.
findings.failure_scenario: systemd runs the three `ExecStart=` lines of a Type=oneshot unit sequentially and aborts the sequence on the first non-zero exit (no `-` prefix on any of them). `cmd_run_once` raises SystemExit — i.e. exit 1 — on states that are ordinary rather than exceptional for a dispatcher fired every 15 s: `max_account_orchestrator.py:1077` 'pending manifest profile(s) are busy with active job(s)', :1065 'no eligible/probed account', :1059 'exhausted attempts'. On every such tick, ExecStart line 12 (`record-done`, the step that runs `coordinator record-output-batch` and commits finished job output, cmd_record_done at :930-997) never executes. A job that completed while another profile was busy sits unharvested until a tick where run-once happens to succeed; if the roster stays saturated or an account is permanently ineligible, that tick never comes and paid output is stranded. Nothing alerts: the only signal is a `failed` unit state and an unrotated append-only log (lines 13-14, no logrotate anywhere in the repo).
findings.evidence: pwg-ru-max-orchestrator.service:10-12 — three bare `ExecStart=` lines, none prefixed with `-`. `max_account_orchestrator.py:1074-1077`: `if busy_rows:\n    detail = ...\n    raise SystemExit('pending manifest profile(s) are busy with active job(s): %s' % detail)`.
findings.existing_test_gap: The runtime-contract CI lane (ci.yml:235-272) runs `max_account_orchestrator_selftest.py` in-process, one subcommand at a time; nothing models the three-command systemd sequence or asserts that record-done is reachable when run-once refuses. No unit-file lint exists.
findings.fix_boundary: RussianTranslation/deploy/pwg-ru-max-orchestrator.service — prefix the dispatch line with `-`, or split recover/run-once/record-done into separately-triggered units; alternatively make cmd_run_once return 0 with a printed reason for the 'nothing to dispatch' states and reserve non-zero for genuine faults.

corrections: The residual true statement, stripped of the refuted scenario: "In `pwg-ru-max-orchestrator.service`, no `ExecStart=` line carries a `-` prefix, so any non-zero exit from line 11 (`run-once`) skips line 12 (`record-done`) for that tick." That is a design nit, not a P1 data-loss defect. It cannot strand output on its own — the states that make `run-once` exit non-zero all raise before any job is claimed (:1053, :1058, :1064), and the busy-state exit at :1077 is dead code under this unit because line 10's unscoped `recover` clears every `in_progress` row first. Stranding needs a prior compound fault (release_runtime non-zero after a sibling job reached `done`, or a `record-done` failure) AND a permanently-refusing successor tick, and even then it is delay, not loss: `record-done` is an idempotent catch-up batch that the runbook documents as a standalone operator command. The blast radius is also hypothetical — the unit has never been installed (four-profile is NO-GO, profiles unauthenticated); the live path is `cmd_staged_run`. If the fix is wanted anyway, the cheap correct one is `-` on line 11, or returning 0 with a printed reason for the nothing-to-dispatch states.

Two corrections. (1) The finding's headline mechanism is wrong for this unit: the :1077 'profile(s) are busy with active job(s)' refusal cannot fire through the systemd sequence, because ExecStart line 10 runs `recover`, whose UPDATE at max_account_orchestrator.py:890-894 unconditionally resets EVERY state='in_progress' row to 'pending' before line 11 queries state='in_progress' at :1069-1072 — busy_rows is empty by construction in the same tick. The reachable refusals are :1054 (no valid profile binding), :1065 (no eligible/probed account — the realistic one, reached via the rate-limit park at :548-551, and the one I reproduced) and the post-dispatch release_runtime SystemExit at :1131-1135, which is the cleanest same-tick stranding (job A reaches 'done' while job B's runtime release fails). :1059 (exhausted attempts) is near-unreachable in practice, since fail_or_retry (:366) marks such jobs 'failed' and requeue_rate_limited (:411-427) decrements attempts precisely so a pending row never sits at max. (2) Severity: P1 assumes a running dispatcher. The unit is installed on no known host and the four-account Max lane has never gone live, so this is a latent defect in an uninstalled deployment file, and even under deployment the stranding is time-bounded by the park's reset epoch (5 h default) rather than permanent.

findings.lead_adjudication: Both lenses agree the unit file is as quoted (three unprefixed ExecStart lines, Type=oneshot) and both refuse the finding's stated mechanism on the same ground: the ':1077 profile(s) are busy' refusal is DEAD CODE under this unit, because ExecStart line 10 runs `recover` with no scope flags and its UPDATE resets every state='in_progress' row to 'pending' before line 11 ever queries in_progress. Reproduction then found a different, genuinely reachable path and drove it on a fixture: with one account parked after a 429, `run-once` exits 1 at :1065 ('no eligible/probed account'), line 12 never runs, and running `record-done` by hand on that same DB harvests the job. So the invariant is violated by the unit as written. What removes the severity is deployment: on the prod box there is no /opt/factory, no /var/lib/pwg-ru, no /var/log/pwg-ru and no such unit installed — the only PWG systemd pair present is a disabled single-ExecStart `pwg-lane` timer — and .ai_state.md:1756 records the four-account Max lane as LIVE-PROOF BLOCKED. Ruling: PLAUSIBLE at P3, retitled to the reachable refusal, with the busy-check mechanism struck. Fix before the unit is ever installed, not now.
